identification.summary: Iranian nation-state threat actor that Microsoft tracks as Peach Sandstorm (formerly HOLMIUM), whose activity overlaps with public reporting on APT33, Elfin and Refined Kitten [S1]. Microsoft assesses that it operates on behalf of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and conducts long-running intelligence collection [S2]. Since 2023 its signature tradecraft has been large-scale password spraying followed by cloud-focused post-compromise activity in Microsoft Entra ID and Azure [S1][S2]. Older vendor reporting describes a group focused on aviation and petrochemical-linked energy targets in Saudi Arabia, the US and South Korea [S4].
identification.firstObserved: FireEye (as reported) tracked APT33 activity since at least May 2016 [S4]; the imported Mandiant summary on this record says cyber espionage since at least 2013 (no cited primary located). Microsoft cites a 2019 password-spray wave and continuous spraying since at least February 2023 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Peach Sandstorm (formerly HOLMIUM). Microsoft states overlap, not identity, with APT33 (Mandiant/FireEye), Elfin (Symantec) and Refined Kitten (CrowdStrike) [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as APT33 (G0064) [S8]. Facts from APT33/Elfin-era reporting (2016-2019) are kept attributed to those vendors and are not merged into Microsoft's Peach Sandstorm findings.

attribution.sponsor: Islamic Republic of Iran; Microsoft assesses Peach Sandstorm operates on behalf of the IRGC [S2]. FireEye (as reported in 2017) assessed APT33 works on behalf of the Iranian government [S4].
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessments only. Microsoft's 2024 IRGC assessment is based on victimology and operational focus and carries no stated confidence level [S2]; its 2023 report describes an 'Iranian nation-state threat actor' and assesses the campaign is 'likely' used for intelligence collection [S1]. No US government attribution was located in this research pass.
attribution.basis: Victimology and operational focus [S2]; activity patterns aligned with Iranian working hours (09:00-17:00 IRST) in May-June 2023 [S1]; FireEye's 2017 analysis of targeting and tooling, as reported [S4].

objectives: Intelligence collection in support of Iranian state interests, with Microsoft assessing its initial-access campaigns are likely used to facilitate that collection [S1][S2]. Satellite, defense, government and oil-and-gas targeting suggests interest in military, space and energy information [S2]. Earlier vendors noted destructive capability: FireEye reported the SHAPESHIFT wiper in APT33's toolkit but had not seen it used destructively [S4], and Symantec said Elfin shifted from data destruction toward data theft [S5].

sectors: Oil and gas / energy, including petrochemical [S2][S4]
Historic: construction, financial services, healthcare, telecommunications [S1]
targeting.notes: Microsoft says the 2023 password spray hit thousands of organizations across several sectors and geographies and that a subset was opportunistic [S1]; the follow-on intrusions focus on a narrower set of high-value targets [S1][S2]. Trend Micro reported narrowly targeted 2019 botnets with victims including a US national-security services company, US universities and a likely US military-related victim [S6].

capabilities.summary: Initial access: high-volume password spraying from TOR and commercial VPN infrastructure using a 'go-http-client' user agent [S1][S2]; attempted exploitation of public PoCs for Zoho ManageEngine CVE-2022-47966 and Confluence CVE-2022-26134 [S1]; LinkedIn personas posing as students, developers and recruiters from at least November 2021 to mid-2024 [S2]; spear-phishing with job-themed lures and WinRAR CVE-2018-20250 in earlier reporting [S4][S5]. Cloud tradecraft: Entra ID reconnaissance with AzureHound and ROADtools, Azure Arc for persistence on on-premises hosts, the custom EagleRelay tunneling tool on VMs in compromised subscriptions, and a Golden SAML attack using stolen AD FS keys in March 2023 [S1]; C2 hosted in fraudulent Azure subscriptions created via Azure for Students or compromised education-tenant accounts [S2]. Malware: the Tickler multi-stage backdoor (2024), which uses DLL sideloading and a Run key for persistence [S2]; the FalseFont backdoor aimed at defense industrial base personnel (late 2023) [S3]; and in older reporting the DROPSHOT dropper, SHAPESHIFT wiper and TURNEDUP backdoor [S4]. Post-compromise: AnyDesk, AD Explorer snapshots, SMB and RDP lateral movement, and DLL search-order hijacking of a VMware executable [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Aviation and petrochemical espionage (FireEye APT33)
campaigns.summary: FireEye reported spear-phishing against a US aerospace firm, a Saudi conglomerate with aviation holdings and a South Korean petrochemical company, using job-vacancy lures and DROPSHOT/TURNEDUP tooling (reported as active from at least May 2016).

campaigns.name: Elfin campaign (Symantec)
campaigns.summary: Symantec described a multi-year Elfin campaign against Saudi and US organizations, including exploitation of WinRAR CVE-2018-20250 against a Saudi chemical-sector organization; it found no further evidence tying Elfin to the Shamoon attacks.

campaigns.name: Narrow-targeting botnets (Trend Micro)
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reported about a dozen live C2 servers running small botnets for persistence inside selected targets in the Middle East, US and Asia.

campaigns.name: LinkedIn persona operations
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports fake LinkedIn profiles for intelligence gathering and possible social engineering against higher education, satellite and defense targets from at least November 2021 to mid-2024.

campaigns.name: Global password spray campaign
campaigns.summary: February-July 2023 password spraying against thousands of organizations, followed by Entra ID reconnaissance, Azure Arc persistence, EagleRelay, a March 2023 Golden SAML intrusion and data exfiltration in a small number of cases.

campaigns.name: FalseFont backdoor against defense industrial base
campaigns.summary: Microsoft (as reported) observed Peach Sandstorm attempting to deliver the FalseFont backdoor to individuals in the defense industrial base; the malware was first seen around early November 2023.

campaigns.name: Tickler backdoor intelligence-gathering operations
campaigns.summary: April-July 2024 deployment of Tickler against satellite, communications equipment, oil and gas and government targets in the US and UAE, with password spraying in the US and Australia and C2 on fraudulent Azure subscriptions.

diamond.adversary: Iranian nation-state actor assessed by Microsoft to operate on behalf of the IRGC [S2]; overlaps APT33/Elfin/Refined Kitten [S1].
diamond.capability: Password spraying; Entra ID reconnaissance (AzureHound, ROADtools); Azure Arc; EagleRelay; Golden SAML; Tickler and FalseFont backdoors; historic DROPSHOT, SHAPESHIFT and TURNEDUP [S1][S2][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: TOR and commercial VPN egress for spraying; fraudulent or compromised Azure subscriptions and azurewebsites.net C2 domains; VMs in victim subscriptions for tunneling; fake LinkedIn profiles [S1][S2]; small dedicated botnets and C2 servers in 2019 [S6].
diamond.victim: Satellite, defense, government, oil and gas, communications-equipment, higher-education and pharmaceutical organizations in the US, UAE, Australia, Europe and the Middle East [S1][S2]; historically aviation and petrochemical firms in Saudi Arabia, the US and South Korea [S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection supporting Iranian state and IRGC interests [S2]; Microsoft notes a 2019 spray wave coincided with US-Iran tensions [S1].
diamond.technology: Cloud identity (Microsoft Entra ID/Microsoft 365), AD FS, Azure subscriptions, internet-facing Confluence and ManageEngine servers, and Microsoft Teams as a delivery channel [S1][S2].

gaps: No US government attribution or advisory specific to Peach Sandstorm/APT33 was located in this pass; IRGC sponsorship rests on Microsoft's assessment [S2].
FalseFont details rely on press coverage of Microsoft's December 2023 social-media disclosure; no Microsoft blog post was opened, and the delivery method was not disclosed [S3].
FireEye/Mandiant 2017 APT33 report and Symantec 2019 Elfin report were not opened directly; facts come from news coverage [S4][S5].
Victim counts in the Symantec Elfin report differ across coverage (one outlet cites 50 organizations, another 18 US organizations); unresolved.
Reported links to the Nasr Institute (2017 coverage) and to the Shamoon/StoneDrill wiper attacks are unproven; Symantec said it found no further evidence tying Elfin to Shamoon [S4][S5].
The imported claim of activity 'since at least 2013' could not be tied to a primary source in this pass.
No vendor primary reporting on Peach Sandstorm activity in 2025-2026 was found; a November 2025 third-party forecast (Brandefense) was not used.
Trend Micro's 2019 report could not be fetched; relied on search excerpts [S6].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Cloud identity planes (Entra ID, AD FS, Azure subscriptions) are key terrain because Peach Sandstorm's access and persistence run through them [S1][S2]; satellite, defense and DIB contractor tenants and university partners are part of the relevant environment [S2][S3]. STEP 2 (effects): Weak or legacy authentication and unmonitored Azure resource creation make spray-and-pivot attacks cheap; compromised education tenants can host C2 that blends with legitimate azurewebsites.net traffic [S2]. STEP 3 (threat model): password spray from TOR/VPN, then Entra ID reconnaissance (AzureHound/ROADtools), then persistence via new subscriptions, Azure Arc, AnyDesk or Tickler, then lateral movement over SMB/RDP and data collection [S1][S2]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued low-cost spraying and LinkedIn persona approaches against space, defense and government personnel to collect military and satellite information [S2]. MDCOA, inferred from historic wiper tooling [S4], is use of established access in a crisis to stage destructive effects against defense or energy-sector networks. Candidate indicators: bursts of failed sign-ins with a 'go-http-client' user agent from TOR or VPN IPs; sign-ins concentrated in 09:00-17:00 IRST; unexpected Azure Arc agents or new Azure subscriptions; AD FS key access; Run keys for 'SharePoint.exe' outside expected paths; outbound traffic to unfamiliar azurewebsites.net hosts; AD Explorer use [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: identity telemetry (Entra ID sign-in and audit logs, Azure subscription and Arc events) should feed the common operational picture, because much of this actor's activity is invisible to endpoint-only sensors [S1][S2]. (2) Authorities: C2 often sits in commercially hosted Azure subscriptions rather than adversary-owned servers, so disruption depends on coordination with the cloud provider [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: satellite operators, space and DIB contractors supporting Air Force missions are named targets; their tenants are a mission dependency [S2][S3]. (4) Coordination: share spray indicators and fake-persona reporting with DC3/DIB CS partners and with academic partners whose tenants may be abused [S2].
